title: Answering a Check the AI Question
blurb: What a 2-point answer needs: say what the chart really shows, and why it matters. ChatGPT is sometimes right.

steps.title: How these questions work
steps.html:
• You see three things: a chart, the exact prompt we gave ChatGPT, and ChatGPT's answer word for word (with a screen recording as proof). Your job is to judge the answer against the chart, not against what you expect the data to say.
  • ChatGPT can be right, wrong, or right but incomplete. If it is right, say so and point to what in the chart confirms it: "I agree, because …" can earn full credit. In this review, the garage heat map (Color) and the stacked bars (Commonly Used Charts) are cases where ChatGPT is right.
  • A 2-point answer has two parts. One point for saying what the chart actually shows: what ChatGPT got right, got wrong, or left out. One point for why it matters: what a reader would wrongly conclude, or what you would check or fix.
  • "I agree" or "I disagree" alone earns 0. So does repeating ChatGPT's answer in other words.
  • Keep it to 2 or 3 sentences. Name the specific thing in the chart (an axis, a group of points, a line, a color, a legend), not a general rule.
  • Pasting the question into an AI is allowed, but its answer is one more reading to check. The same chart can get different answers from one run to the next.

Every "Check the AI" question in the units that follow uses this format, and the feedback while you type checks the same two parts.

title: Honest Charts
blurb: Truncated axes, the lie factor, data-ink and dual axes: when a chart's drawing says more than its data.

steps.title: What to remember
steps.html:
• Bars must start at zero. A bar shows its value by its length. If the axis starts at 11,000, a bar for 12,000 is drawn one unit long and a bar for 15,000 four units long, although 15,000 is only 25% more.
  • Lines may start above zero when the change is the point, because a line shows values by position and slope, not by length. Label the axis so the reader sees where it starts.
  • Lie factor = the size of the effect shown in the graphic ÷ the size of the effect in the data. Near 1 is honest. A lie factor of 4 means the chart makes the change look four times as big as it is.
  • Data-ink. Ink that does not show data (3D, heavy grids, decoration) competes with the ink that does. Remove it.
  • Dual axes let the designer choose two scales, so any two series can be made to look as if they move together.

title: Data Types and Encodings
blurb: Nominal, ordinal and quantitative variables, the channels that suit each, and the grammar of graphics as a vocabulary.

steps.title: What to remember
steps.html:
• Data types. Nominal: names with no order (bowl game yes or no, a major). Ordinal: ordered labels (1st, 2nd, 3rd in the conference). Quantitative (interval or ratio): numbers you can subtract (points per game, wins).
  • Channels, best first for numbers: position on a common scale, then length, then angle and area, then color intensity. Hue (different colors) and shape are for categories, because they have no order.
  • The grammar of graphics names the parts of any chart: the data, the aesthetics (which variable goes to x, y, color, size, shape), the geom (points, bars, lines), scales, facets and coordinates.
  • To read a chart, list each variable and its channel. The axes give two; the legends give the rest. One mark per row: here, one point per season.

steps.title: Five variables in one scatter plot
steps.prompt: Check ChatGPT's list against the chart. Is it right? Then pick one variable and say whether its channel suits its data type.
hints: Check each pair against the axes and the three legends, and name one you checked.

charts.caption: Real data: the Miami football record book (the Game Day file).

ai.answer:

Points allowed per game: Vertical position (y-axis).

Bowl game participation: Color (red/gray).

MAC championship: Shape (triangle/circle).

Number of wins: Bubble size.

Season (year): One mark per season; not visually encoded.

title: Color
blurb: Sequential, diverging and qualitative schemes, and how to tell when a chart picked the wrong one.

steps.title: What to remember
steps.html:
• Sequential: light to dark in one hue, for ordered values from low to high (counts, rates, minutes).
  • Diverging: two hues that meet at a meaningful middle (zero, an average, a target), for values above and below it (change from last year, profit and loss).
  • Qualitative: unrelated hues of similar lightness, for categories with no order (majors, dining halls).
  • Common mistakes: rainbow or qualitative colors on ordered data (the reader cannot tell which color means more without the legend), a diverging scheme with no meaningful middle, and red next to green (about 1 man in 12 cannot tell them apart).

steps.title: A garage heat map
steps.prompt: ChatGPT says this is a qualitative scheme on ordered data. Is it right? Point to something in the chart that shows the problem.
hints: Do the six colors go from light to dark?
Which color means the fewest cars?

charts.alt: Heat map of cars parked in a campus garage by weekday and hour, with six bins from 0 to 100 up to over 500, each bin in an unrelated color: red, blue, green, purple, orange, brown

ai.prompt: This heat map shows the average number of cars parked in a Miami University campus garage for each hour of the week. What type of color scheme does it use, and is that a good choice for this data? Please limit your answer to 30 words.
ai.answer: It uses a qualitative color scheme for ordered numerical data. This is inappropriate because colors lack a natural progression. A sequential color scheme would better communicate increasing parking occupancy.

title: Commonly Used Charts
blurb: Pies, donuts, stacked bars and waterfalls: what each one makes easy, and what it hides.

steps.title: What to remember
steps.html:
• Pies and donuts show values by angle and area, which people compare poorly. With close values, bars on a common baseline win (Pie on Trial).
  • Stacked bars: only the bottom segment and the total sit on the baseline. Middle segments float, so comparing one of them across years means subtracting its bottom edge from its top edge by eye. Instead, show two charts side by side (one for the total, one for the categories as side-by-side bars), or a paneled bar chart with one panel per category.
  • No bars for averages: a bar suggests that the data sit inside it, and it hides how spread out they are. Show the points instead, with a line at each average, or on top of a box plot.
  • Waterfall: shows how a starting value becomes an ending value through gains and losses.
  • Choose the chart from the question: compare categories (bars), part of a whole (sorted bars of each part's share), change over time (line).

title: Time
blurb: Lines and bars over time, the spacing of the time axis, seasonality, calendar plots, and animation versus small multiples.

steps.title: What to remember
steps.html:
• Lines for continuous time, where the trend is the story. Bars for a few separate periods you compare one by one. With only two time points, a line draws a path between them that was never measured.
  • Check the spacing of the time axis. If years are skipped but drawn the same distance apart, every slope is bent. Compare the change per year, or put time on a real time axis.
  • Seasonality is a pattern that repeats every year (semesters, breaks, holidays). To judge growth, compare the same month across years, not neighboring months.
  • Calendar plots lay daily values out like a calendar, so day-of-week and month patterns stand out.
  • Animation or small multiples. Animation (Rosling's Gapminder) draws attention but asks the viewer to remember earlier frames. Small multiples put every time point side by side for comparison.

title: Maps
blurb: Choropleths, proportional symbols and cartograms, and why a map of counts is often a map of population.

steps.title: What to remember
steps.html:
• Choropleth: each region filled with a color. Use it for rates or shares (per resident, per 10,000), not raw counts, or the map mostly shows where people live.
  • Proportional symbols: a circle per region, sized by a count. This suits totals.
  • Cartogram: regions resized by a variable such as population, so small, crowded places are not hidden by large empty ones.
  • Before reading a map of counts, ask how many people live in each region. Franklin, Cuyahoga and Hamilton hold about a third of Ohio's people, so they lead almost any count.

steps.prompt: Do you agree with ChatGPT? What did it miss? Say what this map really shows, and what you would need to answer the question.

title: Many Variables
blurb: Small multiples, parallel coordinates, radar charts, heat maps and treemaps.

steps.title: What to remember
steps.html:
• Small multiples: the same small chart once per group. Check whether the panels share an axis. With separate axes (scales = "free_y"), every panel fills its box and big and small groups look alike.
  • Parallel coordinates: one vertical axis per variable, one line per observation. Lines that cross between two axes show a negative relationship; lines that run parallel show a positive one.
  • Radar: parallel coordinates wrapped into a circle. The shape depends on the order of the axes.
  • Heat map: a grid of rows and columns with each cell colored by its value.
  • Treemap: nested rectangles sized by value, for parts of a whole with a hierarchy.

title: Is the Data Right?
blurb: Five charts that read cleanly and still mislead, because of how the data were recorded or counted.

steps.title: What to remember
steps.html:
• An AI describes the chart it is shown. It rarely asks whether the data could be right. That part is yours.
  • Question 1: does the pattern follow the business, or the reporting schedule? Ohio's COVID line (Class 21) went up and down every week because counties reported on fixed days, not because the virus did. The Class 22 check-in had the same comb.
  • Question 2: what is one row, and could something be counted twice? In a course file with one row per section, Tableau's SUM added a campus's enrollment once for every section listed. In the crash file (Class 13), one row is one person involved, not one crash.
  • Compare with what you know. A familiar dataset that suddenly shows the opposite of what you saw in class is a reason to check the data, not a new finding.
  • The data in this unit are simulated or altered for practice, except the crash file, which is the real one from class.

title: Build It
blurb: Answer questions from a CSV in Tableau or Power BI, then improve and rebuild two charts that ChatGPT made from the same file.

steps.title: What the exam asks
steps.html:
The last two exam questions are built in Tableau or Power BI. You get a CSV, answer questions with a chart, and improve two charts that ChatGPT made from the same file. Practice both here with a file of Rec Center visits (simulated, 2,400 rows: one row per visit).

Download rec_center_visits_fall2026.csv (columns: visit_id, date, facility, visitor_type, minutes).

Design checklist (Classes 15 and 16): a title that says what the chart shows, labeled axes with units, bars that start at zero and are sorted, color only when it carries a variable, and no chart junk.

Then a sanity check (Class 19): could each number be true? In Map Gallery, maps that added up the weekly running totals gave Butler County about 7.6 million cases, in a county of fewer than 400,000 people.

steps.title: Answer from the CSV
steps.html:
1. How many visits did each facility have? Make a bar chart, sorted from most to fewest visits.
  2. How does visit length differ by visitor type? Make a chart that shows the spread of minutes for each visitor type, not only an average (Tableau: Show Me, box-and-whisker plot). If your tool cannot draw a box plot, show the median minutes for each visitor type.
steps.check:
Visits by facility: Main gym 734, Fitness studios 567, Courts 556, Pool 343, Climbing wall 200 (2,400 in all).

Median minutes: Undergraduate 63, Graduate 52, Faculty or staff 41. Undergraduates also have the longest visits (the long tail of points above about 130 minutes).

If your counts are off, check that you counted rows (visit_id), not summed the minutes.

steps.title: Improve ChatGPT's two charts
steps.prompt: ChatGPT made these two charts from the same file. Name one improvement for each chart, and say why it helps.
hints: Why is Main gym a different color? What does the title tell you?
Can you read the median labels? How many visits does each box stand for?

charts.alt: ChatGPT's horizontal bar chart titled Visits by facility, sorted, with Main gym highlighted in dark teal and the other bars light gray-blue, values labeled
charts.caption: ChatGPT's chart 1.

charts.alt: ChatGPT's box plot titled Visit length by visitor type, with undergraduate, graduate and faculty or staff boxes in three shades, and median labels that overlap the boxes
charts.caption: ChatGPT's chart 2.

ai.prompt: This file lists visits to Miami University's Recreation Center in September and October 2026 (simulated data), one row per visit. Make two charts: (1) the number of visits by facility, and (2) how visit length in minutes differs by visitor type.
ai.answer:
The dataset contains 2,400 visits to Miami University's Recreation Center during September and October 2026.

The Main gym was the busiest facility, with 734 visits, followed by Fitness studios (567) and Courts (556).

Visit duration also differed by visitor type. Undergraduates had the longest median visits (63 minutes), followed by graduate students (52 minutes) and faculty or staff (41 minutes).

[Chart 1, shown above: Number of visits by facility]

[Chart 2, shown above: Visit length by visitor type]

The second chart uses box plots to show differences in median visit length, variability, and unusually long visits—not just averages.

steps.title: Rebuild them
steps.html: Rebuild both of ChatGPT's charts in Tableau or Power BI with your improvements, from the same CSV.
steps.check:
A good rebuild of chart 1: sorted bars, one color (or a highlight explained in the title, such as "Main gym gets almost a third of all visits"), value labels or a light axis, and the time period in the subtitle.

A good rebuild of chart 2: one box per visitor type in a single color, medians readable (labels beside the boxes or in the axis labels), and the number of visits per group, for example "Undergraduate (n = 1,870)". Undergraduates make up most of the visits, so their box rests on far more data than the faculty or staff box.

steps.html:
Each build below uses a different real data file. Build the chart in Tableau or Power BI, type the numbers it asks for, and paste a screenshot of just your chart. The numbers are checked exactly; the chart is read by an AI model (Jev) that answers a few yes-or-no questions about it, such as "is it sorted?". The chart check is experimental, so if it gets your chart wrong, use "Report a problem".

Each file hides one thing to get right before the numbers come out right. Look at the rows before you build.

Could a reader find the largest and smallest at a glance?
Is the axis a share or a count?

title: Replay the games
blurb: Game Day, Pie on Trial and Race Call at your own pace, with the answers and how the class answered, plus redo cards for Press Time and the Map Gallery.

steps.title: Game Day (Class 16)
steps.html: The 14 questions of Game Day at Yager, in the order they were played: distortion, data-ink and data types, encodings and color, and the grammar of graphics. Pick an answer and press Check to see the answer and why, and how the class answered. Questions 4 and 14 were open questions: write your answer and it is checked as you type, as in the other units.

steps.title: Game Day 1: What a lie factor of 4 means
steps.prompt: This chart of U.S. adults who describe themselves as Christian has a lie factor of about 4. What does that mean?

charts.alt: Bar chart, U.S. adults who describe themselves as Christian: 77% in 2009 and 65% in 2019. The y-axis runs from 58% to 78%.
charts.caption: From Game Day, Class 16.

options: The values are off by about 4 percentage points
The drop looks about 4 times as large as it really is
The chart shows the drop at about a quarter of its real size
About 4 of the values on the chart are wrong
steps.why: Lie factor = the size of the change in the graphic divided by the size of the change in the data. The data dropped from 77% to 65%, which is 15.6% of 77. On an axis that starts at 58%, the bar shrinks from 19 points tall to 7, which is 63.2%. 63.2 / 15.6 = about 4: the drop looks about 4 times as large as it is.
steps.source: Pew Research Center (2019), values shown in a Fox News chart with a y-axis from 58%; redrawn. https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2019/10/17/in-u-s-decline-of-christianity-continues-at-rapid-pace/ ; https://video.foxnews.com/v/6274513508001

steps.title: Game Day 2: Squares for budgets
steps.prompt: Each square's side is proportional to the country's defense budget. By area, how many times larger does Russia's square look than Ukraine's?

charts.alt: Two squares, Defense budgets, 2020 (US$ billion): a large square for Russia, $60.6B, and a tiny square for Ukraine, $4.32B.
charts.caption: From Game Day, Class 16.

steps.why: The sides are in proportion to the budgets: 60.6 / 4.32 = 14 times. But the eye compares areas, and the area grows with the side squared: 14 x 14 = about 200. Area is a weak channel for amounts; bars (length) would show 14 times as 14 times.
steps.source: Values printed on a squares chart shared by Cedric Scherer (2022), original outlet unclear; redrawn. https://x.com/CedScherer/status/1498593405408059394

steps.title: Game Day 3: Time of possession
steps.prompt: This chart shows time of possession in Miami's Oct 17, 2026 game against Akron: Miami 27:56, Akron 32:04. What is the main problem with it?

charts.alt: Bar chart of time of possession, Miami vs Akron, Oct 17, 2026: Miami 27:56 and Akron 32:04. The y-axis runs from 27:00 to 33:00.
charts.caption: From Game Day, Class 16.

options: The axis starts at 27:00, not at zero
Clock times are ordinal, so bars do not fit
No problem: Akron had the ball about 5 times as long
No problem: the times are printed on the bars
steps.why: Akron held the ball 32:04 and Miami 27:56: a ratio of 1.15. Drawn from 27:00, the bars are 304 and 56 seconds long, a ratio of about 5.4. A bar's length is its value, so bars must start at zero. Printing the times on the bars does not fix what the eye sees first.
steps.source: Miami vs Akron box score, Oct 17, 2026. https://miamiredhawks.com/sports/football/stats/2026/akron/boxscore/20842

steps.title: Game Day 4: The mining company's chart
steps.prompt: This chart is redrawn from a mining company's annual report. What is misleading about it, and how would you fix it?
hints: Read the 1970 label in the net income panel. Which way does its bar point?
Compare $75,243 with $351,341, or the tallest bars of the three panels.
Say how you would redraw it.

charts.alt: Three panels redrawn from a mining company's annual report: operating revenues, net income (loss), and exploration and development expenditures, 1970 to 1974. Each value is printed above its bar and there is no value axis. The 1970 net income is printed as $(11,014).
charts.caption: From Game Day, Class 16.

steps.title: Game Day 4: the answer shown in class
steps.html: Write your own answer above first. Then compare it with the strong answer the projector showed at the reveal.
steps.check:
What misleads

  • The bars do not start at zero, so heights are not proportional to the dollars: $75,243 looks almost as tall as $351,341.
  • The 1970 net loss of $11,014 is drawn as an upward bar, like a profit.
  • Each panel has its own hidden scale: the tallest bars ($7.38M, $1.65M, $1.23M) are drawn the same height, so comparisons across panels mislead.
  • There is no value axis, so the size of a bar means nothing without its printed label.
  • The dollar labels run sideways, which makes them hard to read.

Fixes

  • Start every bar at zero on a labeled dollar axis.
  • Draw the 1970 loss below (or left of) zero.
  • Show each panel's scale, or put the panels on one common axis to compare across them.
  • Use horizontal bars so the dollar labels read left to right.

steps.title: Game Day 5: Numbers that are labels
steps.prompt:
Six rows of the 2025 RedHawks roster. Which column holds numbers but is nominal?
JerseyPositionClassHeight (in)Weight (lb)Home state
1Defensive BackSr74208KY
8Defensive BackFr70193OH
8Wide ReceiverJr69154GA
9Running BackGr70229IN
22Defensive LineSo76249OK
22Defensive BackFr73194PA
steps.why: A jersey number is a label: two players wear #8 and two wear #22, and the average jersey number means nothing. Height and weight are ratio (a true zero); class is ordinal and is not a number at all.
steps.source: Miami RedHawks 2025 football roster (names removed). https://miamiredhawks.com/sports/football/roster/2025

steps.title: Game Day 6: Class year
steps.prompt: The roster lists each player's class year as Fr, So, Jr, Sr or Gr. Which type of variable is class year?
steps.why: Fr, So, Jr, Sr and Gr have a natural order, but the distance between two levels is not a measured amount. Ordered categories without measured distances are ordinal.
steps.source: Miami RedHawks 2025 football roster. https://miamiredhawks.com/sports/football/roster/2025 ; Stevens (1946), On the theory of scales of measurement. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.103.2684.677

steps.title: Game Day 7: Crowds and temperatures
steps.prompt: Akron game: 18,515 fans, 53 °F kickoff. Holy Cross game: 11,126 fans, 76 °F kickoff. Claim 1: the Akron crowd was 1.66 times the Holy Cross crowd. Claim 2: the Holy Cross kickoff was 43% hotter. Which claims are valid?
steps.why: Attendance has a true zero (no fans), so a ratio means something: 18,515 / 11,126 = 1.66. Zero degrees Fahrenheit is not "no temperature", so degrees are interval: differences work, ratios do not. 76 / 53 = 1.43 does not mean 43% hotter.
steps.source: Box scores: Akron, Oct 17, 2026 (the Family Weekend game) https://miamiredhawks.com/sports/football/stats/2026/akron/boxscore/20842 ; Holy Cross, Sept 12, 2026 https://miamiredhawks.com/sports/football/stats/2026/holy-cross/boxscore/20837 ; Family Weekend, Oct 16-18, 2026: https://miamioh.edu/news/2026/10/family-weekend-puts-focus-on-miami-traditions-oct-16-18.html

steps.title: Game Day 8: Which ink is data?
steps.prompt: Which element of this chart is data-ink?

charts.alt: Bar chart titled MIAMI POINTS PER GAME!! for 2021 to 2025: red bars with thick black outlines and dark shadows, on a green football-field background with white yard lines.
charts.caption: From Game Day, Class 16.

options: The green field behind the bars
The dark shadow beside each bar
The height of each red bar
steps.why: Data-ink is the ink that shows the data, and erasing it would lose information: here, the height of each red bar. The field, the yard lines and the shadows are decoration (chartjunk) and can all go.
steps.source: Miami points per game by season, 2026 Football Record Book (Year-By-Year Records, printed p. 57). https://miamiredhawks.com/documents/2026/6/17/2026_FB_Record_Book.pdf

steps.title: Game Day 9: The most accurate encoding
steps.prompt: You want readers to compare Miami's points per game across seasons as accurately as possible. Which encoding should carry the values?
steps.why: In Cleveland and McGill's experiments, readers judged position along a common axis most accurately. Angle, area and color intensity come much lower, which is why a dot plot or bar chart beats a pie, bubbles or shading for comparing values.
steps.source: Cleveland, W. S., and McGill, R. (1984). Graphical perception. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 79(387), 531-554. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478080

steps.title: Game Day 10: A palette for point differential
steps.prompt: You want to color each 2026 game by Miami's point differential, from -45 at Pittsburgh to +38 against Holy Cross. Which kind of palette fits?
steps.why: Point differential has a meaningful middle, 0 (a tie), with losses on one side and wins on the other. Values on both sides of a midpoint need a diverging palette: two hues that get darker away from zero.
steps.source: Miami 2026 schedule and box scores, through Oct 17, 2026. https://miamiredhawks.com/sports/football/schedule/2026

steps.title: Game Day 11: Red and green
steps.prompt: The left chart colors wins green and losses red. The right panel simulates how a reader with deuteranopia sees it. What is the best fix?

charts.alt: Two panels of horizontal bars, Miami points by game in 2026 for seven opponents. Left, as drawn: wins in green and losses in red. Right, the same chart as a reader with deuteranopia sees it: wins and losses are the same olive color.
charts.caption: From Game Day, Class 16.

options: Use a brighter red for the losses
Make the bars wider so the colors show
Use blue and orange, and label W or L
steps.why: Under deuteranopia, red and green look alike, so a brighter red or wider bars do not help. Blue and orange stay apart for most readers with a color vision deficiency, and a W or L label works without any color at all.
steps.source: Miami 2026 schedule, through Oct 17, 2026 (https://miamiredhawks.com/sports/football/schedule/2026); simulation with colorspace::deutan (Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes, 2009, https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2009.113).

steps.title: Game Day 12: What fill shows
steps.prompt: In this chart, which variable is mapped to fill?

charts.alt: Bar chart of points by quarter, Miami vs Akron, Oct 17, 2026: quarters Q1 to Q4 on the x-axis, points on the y-axis, red bars for Miami and gray bars for Akron side by side, with a legend.
charts.caption: From Game Day, Class 16.

steps.why: The legend names the two fill colors: Miami and Akron. Quarter is on the x-axis and points on the y-axis: aes(x = quarter, y = points, fill = team) with geom_col(position = "dodge").
steps.source: Miami vs Akron box score, scoring by quarter, Oct 17, 2026. https://miamiredhawks.com/sports/football/stats/2026/akron/boxscore/20842

steps.title: Game Day 13: One layer changed
steps.prompt: Chart B was made from the code for Chart A by changing one layer. Which layer?

charts.alt: Share of total yards, Miami vs Akron, Oct 17, 2026. Chart A: one stacked bar per team, split into rushing (red) and passing (gray). Chart B: the same shares drawn as one circle per team.
charts.caption: From Game Day, Class 16.

steps.why: Same data, same mappings, same geom (stacked bars). Chart B adds coord_polar(theta = "y"): the coordinate system wraps each bar into a circle, which is how ggplot2 makes a pie.
steps.source: Miami vs Akron box score, rushing and passing yards, Oct 17, 2026. https://miamiredhawks.com/sports/football/stats/2026/akron/boxscore/20842

steps.title: Game Day 14: Describe a chart in grammar
steps.prompt: Describe this chart in grammar-of-graphics terms: the aesthetic mappings, the geom, and one more layer.
hints: What sets bar length, what sets the position on the other axis, and what sets the color?
What kind of mark draws each game?
Look at the panels, the colors and the line at zero.

charts.alt: Horizontal bar chart, Miami point differential by game, 2026: seven opponents on the y-axis, Miami points minus opponent points on the x-axis, a vertical line at zero, bars filled red for home and gray for away, in two panels: Non-conference and MAC.
charts.caption: From Game Day, Class 16.

steps.title: Game Day 14: the answer shown in class
steps.html: Write your own answer above first. Then compare it with the strong answer the projector showed at the reveal.
steps.check:
Data

  • Miami's 2026 games through Oct 17, one row per game.

Mappings (aes)

  • x = point differential (Miami points minus opponent points)
  • y = opponent
  • fill = site (home or away), not win or loss: Bowling Green was a home loss

Geom

  • Bars (geom_col)

More layers

  • Facets: separate panels for non-conference and MAC games
  • A reference line at zero (geom_vline)
  • A fill scale: red for home, gray for away

In ggplot2: ggplot(games, aes(x = margin, y = opponent, fill = site)) + geom_col() + geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + facet_grid(conference ~ .)

steps.title: Press Time (Class 18) and the Map Gallery (Class 19)
steps.html: The two build challenges, to do again on your own. Each card gives the task and the data; open Check your work when you are done.

steps.title: Press Time: redo it
steps.html:
Press Time, Class 18. In 15 minutes, with Tableau (or Power BI) and covid_cases_county.csv (on Canvas, the Class 18 file), make:

  1. a map of the total number of COVID cases by county; and
  2. a table of the population of the counties in Ohio.

Then read Butler County, OH's two numbers off your own work: its total cases (hover over it on the map) and its population (its row in the table). Save the workbook so someone else could open it.

Before you drag a measure: what is one row of this file?
steps.check:
Butler County, OH: 113,510 cases and 383,134 people. Cases are the running total on the last date, 2022-12-31.

The SUM trap. One row is one county on one day, and Butler County has 1,023 rows. Its population, 383,134, is on every one of them, so Tableau's default SUM adds it 1,023 times: 391,946,082 people, more than the 328,833,722 in the whole United States. Confirmed cases is already a running total, so SUM adds 1,023 running totals: 53,038,207.

  • Population was added 1,023 times. Any of MIN, MAX, AVG or ATTR gives 383,134.
  • Confirmed cases is a running total. Use MAX, or filter to the latest date.
  • Eight Butler Counties. Put State on the map, or filter to Ohio.

A .twb file holds only the instructions for the views. A .twbx packs the data in with it, so someone else can open your work.

In class: 5% of the 43 analysts reported Butler's cases right; 12% of the 43 analysts reported its population right.

steps.title: Map Gallery: redo it
steps.html:
Map Gallery, Class 19. The question: How did Butler County's COVID experience compare with the rest of Ohio?

Data: ohio_covid_weekly.csv and ohio_counties.geojson (on Canvas, the Class 19 files). One row per Ohio county per week, March 2020 to December 2022, with the columns date, state, county, population and confirmed_cases.

  1. Plan first, before any AI tool: who the map is for and what they should take away; the number each county shows; the time period; how Butler County will stand out; colors and legend; a title; one creative idea; and your first prompt to the AI.
  2. Build a choropleth map with any AI chat tool, Tableau or Power BI. Keep count of your prompts.
  3. Check your plan and your map against the points behind the button.
steps.check:
The points the plans were checked against in class:

  1. Cases are a running total: map the latest week (or the maximum, or week-to-week changes), never the weeks added up.
  2. A rate, not a count: cases per 100,000 residents (cases divided by population), so large counties do not stand out just for their size.
  3. A title that says what is shown (the measure, the place, the period) or states the finding.
  4. Butler County singled out: an outline, a highlight, a label or a callout.
  5. A sequential scale (one hue, light to dark), or a diverging scale centered on Butler County's value.
  6. Change over time: a line chart, small multiples, several dates or an animation.
  7. A finishing touch: a source caption, key words emphasized, or a styling choice of your own.
  8. Some rate values on the map itself, such as Butler County's or the highest.
  9. A clean map: no needless gridlines, axes or clutter.

The classic mistakes: adding up confirmed_cases over the weeks (it is already a running total), and adding up population over the weekly rows.

Numbers to check against (the last week, 2022-12-31): Butler County had 29,627 cases per 100,000 residents, 31st of Ohio's 88 counties from the top; Ohio as a whole had 28,296. The counties ran from Holmes (13,062) to Lawrence (39,118).

In class: 58% of the 38 analysts in class mapped a rate; 100% of the 38 analysts made Butler County stand out.

steps.title: Pie on Trial (Class 20)
steps.html: The two-minute game from Class 20: three sets of values drawn as pies, then the same three as bars. Find the largest slice or bar. The game kept no record of who answered what, so there is no class count here.

steps.title: Race Call (Class 22)
steps.html: The 13 races of Race Call, the election-night chart game that opened Class 22: commonly used charts, time series, maps, and space and time. Race 8 was an animated chart in class; here it is one still frame.

steps.title: Race Call 1: the exit poll's chart
steps.prompt: Election night 2024: the exit poll's most important issue, drawn the way it ran on TV. What kind of chart is this?

charts.alt: Donut chart, most important issue to your vote, national exit poll of 2024 voters: state of democracy 35%, the economy 31%, abortion 14%, immigration 11%, foreign policy 4%, other or no answer 5%, each issue in its own color with a legend.
charts.caption: From Race Call, Class 22.

steps.why: Donut chart. A donut is a pie with its middle cut out, so you compare arc lengths around a hole. Sorted bars show 35% vs 31% at a glance.
steps.source: NBC News national exit poll, 2024 general election, most important issue (as shown on air): https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2024-elections/exit-polls

steps.title: Race Call 2: encoding channels
steps.prompt: Same chart: one nominal variable (the issue) and one quantitative variable (the share). Which encoding channels carry them?

charts.alt: Donut chart, most important issue to your vote, national exit poll of 2024 voters: state of democracy 35%, the economy 31%, abortion 14%, immigration 11%, foreign policy 4%, other or no answer 5%, each issue in its own color with a legend.
charts.caption: From Race Call, Class 22.

options: Issue: color. Share: angle and area
steps.why: Color + angle and area. The issue is a color; the share is an angle (arc) and an area, two of the least accurate channels. A bar chart puts the share on position and length, the most accurate ones.
steps.source: NBC News national exit poll, 2024 general election, most important issue (as shown on air): https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2024-elections/exit-polls

steps.title: Race Call 3: electoral votes, 2020 to 2024
steps.prompt: The Democratic ticket went from 306 electoral votes in 2020 to 226 in 2024. What kind of chart tells that story here?

charts.alt: Chart of the Democratic ticket's electoral votes, 2020 to 2024: a full bar for 306 in 2020, then floating steps for the census (-3) and six states (AZ -11, GA -16, MI -15, NV -6, PA -19, WI -10), ending in a full bar for 226 in 2024. A dashed line marks 270 to win.
charts.caption: From Race Call, Class 22.

options: A bar chart of separate totals
steps.why: Waterfall chart. Each floating bar starts where the last one ended, so the steps add up: 306 - 3 (census) - 77 (six flipped states) = 226. In a bar chart every bar starts at zero.
steps.source: National Archives, Electoral College results 2020 and 2024: https://www.archives.gov/electoral-college/2020 https://www.archives.gov/electoral-college/2024 and Census 2020 apportionment: https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2020/dec/2020-apportionment-data.html

steps.title: Race Call 4: two values
steps.prompt: You have two values: the Republican ticket's electoral votes in 2020 (232) and 2024 (312). Which chart fits better?

charts.alt: Two charts of the Republican ticket's electoral votes: A, a bar chart with 232 in 2020 and 312 in 2024; B, a line chart joining the same two values on a year axis from 2020 to 2024.
charts.caption: From Race Call, Class 22.

options: Either: they say the same thing
steps.why: Bars. A line implies values between the points, so this one claims about 272 votes in 2022, when no election was held. Two separate measurements: compare them with bars.
steps.source: National Archives, Electoral College results 2020 and 2024: https://www.archives.gov/electoral-college/2020 https://www.archives.gov/electoral-college/2024 and Census 2020 apportionment: https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2020/dec/2020-apportionment-data.html

steps.title: Race Call 5: airline passengers per year
steps.prompt: International airline passengers per year, 1949 to 1960. From this chart alone, what can we conclude?

charts.alt: Bar chart of international airline passengers per year (thousands), 1949 to 1960: the bars rise every year, from about 1,500 to about 5,700.
charts.caption: From Race Call, Class 22.

options: It grew by the same amount every year
steps.why: None of the above. Yearly totals cannot show seasons, 12 rising years show no cycle, and the gains ranged from 151 to 574 thousand. By month, a summer peak shows up every year.
steps.source: Box and Jenkins airline passengers, R datasets::AirPassengers: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/datasets/html/AirPassengers.html

steps.title: Race Call 6: one year of job postings
steps.prompt: Indeed job postings in Ohio, 2022 only. They climb into spring, then fall. Does this chart show seasonality?

charts.alt: Line chart of job postings on Indeed in Ohio, 2022 (index, Feb 1, 2020 = 100): it rises from about 153 to about 158 by spring, then falls to about 142 in December.
charts.caption: From Race Call, Class 22.

options: No: one year cannot show a pattern that repeats each year
Yes: the line goes up, then down
No: an index cannot be seasonal
steps.why: No: one year is not enough. Seasonality is a calendar pattern that repeats year after year, so you need several years to see it. Through August 2026, the 2022 hump never came back: it was the turn into a long decline.
steps.source: Indeed Hiring Lab, Job Postings on Indeed in Ohio (IHLIDXUSOH), via FRED: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IHLIDXUSOH

steps.title: Race Call 7: a calendar of crashes
steps.prompt: A calendar plot of traffic crashes per day in Cincinnati, 2025 (darker = more). Which pattern does it show best?

charts.alt: Calendar plot of traffic crashes per day in Cincinnati, 2025: a small grid per month, each square one day, columns running Sunday to Saturday, darker red for more crashes.
charts.caption: From Race Call, Class 22.

steps.why: Weekends are lighter. A calendar plot lines the days of the week up in columns, so a weekly rhythm shows as stripes: 43.8 crashes on an average weekday, 34 on a weekend day. The worst month was October, the worst day Friday.
steps.source: City of Cincinnati Open Data, Traffic Crash Reports (CPD), unique crashes per day: https://data.cincinnati-oh.gov/Safety/Traffic-Crash-Reports-CPD-/rvmt-pkmq

steps.title: Race Call 8: a motion chart
steps.prompt: A motion chart of 142 countries, 1952 to 2007: income, life expectancy, population, continent. What is time mapped to?

charts.alt: One frame (2007) of a motion chart of 142 countries: income per person on a log x-axis, life expectancy on the y-axis, bubble size for population, color for continent, and the year in large type behind the bubbles.
charts.caption: One still frame (2007) of the motion chart from Race Call. In class it played from 1952 to 2007, one frame after another.

options: The animation: each frame is a year
steps.why: The frames. x = income per person (log scale), y = life expectancy, size = population, color = continent, and time = the frames. Motion grabs attention, but comparing years means remembering frames you no longer see.
steps.source: Gapminder data via the gapminder R package (Bryan): https://cran.r-project.org/package=gapminder

steps.title: Race Call 9: county results map
steps.prompt: 2024 presidential results: each of the 3,153 counties is filled with the winner's color. What kind of map is this?

charts.alt: U.S. map of the 2024 presidential results by county: each county filled red where Trump won and blue where Harris won. Red covers most of the land; Alaska and Connecticut are gray.
charts.caption: From Race Call, Class 22.

steps.why: Choropleth. A choropleth fills existing regions with a color for each region's value. The regions keep their land area, so big, empty counties get the most ink.
steps.source: County results compiled by Tony McGovern: https://github.com/tonmcg/US_County_Level_Election_Results_08-24 and county outlines from the Urban Institute's urbnmapr: https://github.com/UrbanInstitute/urbnmapr

steps.title: Race Call 10: land and votes
steps.prompt: Same map: red covers about 85% of the land shown. What share of the national vote did the red candidate get?

charts.alt: U.S. map of the 2024 presidential results by county: each county filled red where Trump won and blue where Harris won. Red covers most of the land; Alaska and Connecticut are gray.
charts.caption: From Race Call, Class 22.

steps.why: About 50%. Land does not vote. Trump won 85% of counties and 85% of the mapped land, but only about half of the national vote. A symbol map sizes circles by votes, so cities finally show up.
steps.source: County results compiled by Tony McGovern: https://github.com/tonmcg/US_County_Level_Election_Results_08-24 and county outlines from the Urban Institute's urbnmapr: https://github.com/UrbanInstitute/urbnmapr

steps.title: Race Call 11: a color scheme for margins
steps.prompt: Each Ohio county's 2024 margin runs from Harris +32 to Trump +69, and 0 is a tie. Which color scheme fits?

charts.alt: Three maps of Ohio's 2024 margin by county (Trump % minus Harris %): Map A with a different unordered color for each range, Map B in one purple hue from light to dark, Map C in blue and red on either side of white.
charts.caption: From Race Call, Class 22.

options: Map B: sequential, light to dark
Map C: diverging, two hues from a middle
Any of them: color is color
steps.why: Diverging. A margin has a meaningful middle (a tie) and two directions, so it needs a diverging scheme. Sequential fits values that only go up, like a share; nominal colors fit unordered groups, never numbers.
steps.source: County results compiled by Tony McGovern: https://github.com/tonmcg/US_County_Level_Election_Results_08-24 and Ohio county outlines from the Census cartographic boundary file: https://www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files/time-series/geo/cartographic-boundary.html

steps.title: Race Call 12: barley at six sites
steps.prompt: Barley yields at six Minnesota sites, 1931 vs 1932, both years in one panel per site. At five sites 1931 beat 1932. Which site flipped?

charts.alt: Dot plots of barley yield by variety (bushels per acre) at six Minnesota sites: Waseca, Crookston, Morris, University Farm, Duluth and Grand Rapids. Each panel shows ten varieties, with 1932 and 1931 as circles of two colors.
charts.caption: From Race Call, Class 22.

steps.why: Morris. Superimposing both years in each site's panel makes the comparison a glance: Morris averaged 41.5 in 1932 vs 29.3 in 1931. Cleveland suspected its years were swapped in the data.
steps.source: Immer, Hayes and Powers (1934), as lattice::barley; Cleveland, Visualizing Data (1993): https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/lattice/html/barley.html

steps.title: Race Call 13: small multiples or animation
steps.prompt: Weekly COVID cases per 100,000 by Ohio county, six snapshots as small multiples. Compared with animating the same maps, small multiples are better at:

charts.alt: Six small maps of Ohio, weekly COVID cases per 100,000 by county, on Sep 5, 2020; Dec 12, 2020; Jun 5, 2021; Sep 18, 2021; Jan 15, 2022; and Apr 2, 2022, all on one color scale from under 50 to 1,000 or more.
charts.caption: From Race Call, Class 22.

options: Comparing dates side by side, without remembering frames
steps.why: Side-by-side comparison. Small multiples keep every date on screen, so your eye compares them directly. The animation grabs attention but makes you remember frames; the peak week, January 15, 2022, flies by.
steps.source: ISA 401 course data covid_cases_county.csv (the Class 18 and 19 file), Ohio counties by week; county outlines from the Census cartographic boundary file: https://www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files/time-series/geo/cartographic-boundary.html
